# fshy: Databases and KV in full

> Hosted databases, vector stores and key-value stores.

Data as of 2026-11-10, the date of the published data. Version `e7cf1b4a40af`: the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of every record's Markdown, topic by topic in the one order (hosted before self-hosted, then verdict, provider name, record id); it changes whenever a record does.

How to read a record, and the other topics: https://fshy.ajam.dev/llms-full.txt. One line per record: https://fshy.ajam.dev/t/databases-kv.md.

## Cloud Firestore (firestore)

- `databases-kv/firestore` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category document database
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/quotas | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/google.md
- free tier: 1 GiB stored, 50,000 document reads per day, 20,000 writes per day, 20,000 deletes per day, exactly one free database per project | unit: GiB | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 1 GiB stored; a 1 MiB document size limit applies to the engine | source: [1]
- retention: data persists; there is no inactivity deletion on the free quota | source: [1]
- egress: 10 GiB a month of outbound data transfer is included in the free quota; beyond it the transfer is billed at the standard Cloud Firestore network rate, and reads are counted as operations against the daily quota | metered: yes | free allowance: 10 GiB per month | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: a Google account
- interface: rest, graphql
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 50,000 document reads and 20,000 writes per day [1]
  - per-object-cap: 1 GiB stored; exactly one free database per project [1]
- limits note: a project may hold up to 100 databases, but only one is free, so multiple logical databases is a paid feature
- interface detail: a REST and gRPC API with realtime listeners; SDKs for web, mobile and server; a GraphQL-ish query surface is not offered, the REST and gRPC APIs are
- tooling: the Firebase Admin SDK; the gcloud and firebase CLIs; REST
- composes with: 1 GiB of document state with client SDKs and realtime sync, which no other free tier here gives
- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: The one-database rule is the constraint that a multi-tenant design meets first, not the 1 GiB.
- evidence note: the quotas page was read and states 'exactly one free database per project'.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free quota: 1 GiB stored data, 50,000 document reads/day, 20,000 writes/day, 20,000 deletes/day; 'Cloud Firestore allows exactly one free database per project'
- sources:
  - [1] https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/quotas

## Cloudflare D1

- `databases-kv/cloudflare-d1` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category serverless SQLite
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/cloudflare.md
- price USD 0.75/GB-month beyond 5 GB on Workers Paid | parsed USD 750/TB-mo
- free tier: 10 databases; 500 MB per database; 5 GB per account; 5 million rows read per day; 100,000 rows written per day | unit: mixed | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 2,000,000 bytes per row, BLOB or string; 500 MB per database | bytes: 2000000 | source: [2]
- retention: storage persists; Time Travel point-in-time recovery covers 7 days on Free | source: [2] | note: the free limits reset daily at 00:00 UTC
- egress: no egress charge; rows read and rows written are the metered quantities | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: a Cloudflare account
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 100,000 rows written per day on Free [1]
  - request-rate (binding): 5 million rows read per day on Free [1]
  - per-object-cap: 500 MB per database and 5 GB per account; a 2,000,000-byte row ceiling [2]
  - request-rate (binding): 50 queries per Worker invocation on Free; a 30-second maximum query duration [2]
- interface detail: a Worker binding, a REST API and the wrangler CLI
- tooling: wrangler d1; the Cloudflare API; better-sqlite3 style calls inside a Worker
- composes with: per-tenant SQLite in a Worker with a free Postgres as the system of record; 500 MB per database and 10 databases is 5 GB of free relational state
- reliability: at the daily read or write limit the D1 API returns errors; at the storage limit you must delete data before you can insert, alter a table or create an index
- notes: The 100,000 rows written a day is the binding number for any ingest, and it is small: 1.16 rows a second sustained. A full table scan counts every row it scans as a row read, so an unindexed query spends the read budget fast.
- evidence note: the limits and pricing pages were read; nothing was provisioned.
- evidence:
  - [2] 2026-10-22: Free: 10 databases, 500 MB maximum database size, 5 GB per account, Time Travel 7 days, 50 queries per Worker invocation; 2,000,000-byte row maximum; 100,000-byte SQL statement; 30-second query maximum
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free: 5 million rows read/day, 100,000 rows written/day, 5 GB total storage; 'Free limits reset daily at 00:00 UTC'; at the storage limit you must delete data before inserting
- sources:
  - [1] https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/pricing/
  - [2] https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits/

## Qdrant Cloud

- `databases-kv/qdrant-cloud` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding per-object-cap | category vector database
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://qdrant.tech/pricing/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/qdrant.md
- free tier: free tier cluster with 1 GB RAM and 4 GB disk, no high availability, one cluster | unit: GB | metered on: stored-bytes | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 4 GB disk per cluster | source: [1]
- retention: no deletion clock and no exhaustion behaviour is published; the FAQ says only that if data growth exceeds the free tier you 'can easily upgrade'. Nothing states what happens to a cluster that reaches 1 GB of RAM | source: [1] | note: an absence of a failure mode rather than a failure mode, which is weaker evidence than a stated limit
- egress: not published on the pricing page; recorded as a gap | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email or GitHub signup; no card on Free
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - per-object-cap (binding): 4 GB disk per cluster; 1 GB RAM [1]
  - request-rate: one cluster per account on Free [1]
  - request-rate: no connection limit is published for the free tier; recorded as a gap [1]
- interface detail: a REST API and gRPC; Python, JS and Rust clients
- tooling: the qdrant-client libraries over gRPC or REST
- composes with: the largest free vector storage by disk, and the closest thing to a self-managed index without a host
- reliability: no high availability on the free tier, so the single node is the availability
- notes: 4 GB of disk holds roughly 1.4 million vectors at 768 dimensions and 4 bytes per component, before index overhead. That puts the ~1 million vectors in circulation in the right order. The figure comes from arithmetic, not from a measurement. What happens at 1 GB of RAM is not published. The page offers an upgrade and states no refusal, throttle or deletion. That absence is documented, and it is not headroom.
- evidence note: the pricing FAQ was read; the numbers are in the page's own answers.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: 'The free tier includes 1GB RAM and 4GB disk storage'; the free tier is 'limited to 1GB RAM and 4GB disk without high availability'
- sources:
  - [1] https://qdrant.tech/pricing/

## TiDB Cloud Starter

- `databases-kv/tidb-cloud-starter` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category distributed SQL, MySQL compatible
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://www.pingcap.com/pricing/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/pingcap.md
- price USD 0.10 per million RUs beyond the allowance
- free tier: 25 GiB row storage plus 25 GiB columnar storage and 250 million Request Units per month, per organization across up to five instances | unit: GiB | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 25 GiB row storage per organization on the allowance; the FAQ states 5 GiB per instance | source: [1] | note: the two first-party pages disagree on whether the allowance is per instance or per org
- retention: an instance persists while the organization is active; no deletion clock published | source: [2]
- egress: no transfer allowance and no per-GB egress rate is published on the pricing page; recorded as a gap. Traffic is billed through the request-unit and storage meters the page does publish | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email signup for the free allowance; a card only to exceed five instances
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 250 million Request Units per month on the org allowance; the FAQ prints 50 million per instance [1]
  - per-object-cap: 25 GiB row plus 25 GiB columnar per organization; five instances [1]
  - write-gated: a credit card and a spend limit are required to create more than five Starter instances [2]
  - request-rate (binding): 400 concurrent connections per Starter instance, rising to 5,000 with a spending limit; the public-endpoint idle timeout is 340 seconds [3]
- interface detail: the MySQL wire protocol with TLS; a Cloud API and the tiup CLI
- tooling: any MySQL client, the tiup CLI, the Data Migration tool
- composes with: the largest card-free relational allowance found in this class, which is why it is the first row a reader should try
- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: The two pages disagree by a factor of five and the direction matters. 25 GiB per org is the number the pricing page states today; 5 GiB per instance is what the FAQ states. Until one is measured, the conservative reading is 5 GiB per instance and 25 GiB per org across five.
- evidence note: two first-party pages were read and they disagree. The record keeps the conservative per-instance reading and names the disagreement.
- extras:
  - page_disagreement: the docs FAQ's figure is the older per-instance plan and the pricing page's is the current org allowance
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free monthly allowance: 25 GiB row storage, 25 GiB columnar storage, 250M Request Units, per organization across up to five eligible instances; rates beyond from USD 0.10 per million RUs
  - [2] 2026-10-22: 'Always-free monthly quota for up to five TiDB Cloud Starter instances per organization (5 GiB row data + 5 GiB columnar data + 50 million RUs per TiDB Cloud Starter instance)'; 'you can create a maximum of five TiDB Cloud Starter instances by default. To create more ... you need to add a credit card'
- sources:
  - [1] https://www.pingcap.com/pricing/
  - [2] https://docs.pingcap.com/tidbcloud/serverless-faqs/
  - [3] https://docs.pingcap.com/tidbcloud/serverless-limitations/

## Turso (Databases and KV)

- `databases-kv/turso` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding retention-clamped | category SQLite at the edge
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://turso.tech/pricing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/turso.md
- price USD 0.75/GB beyond 9 GB on Developer
- free tier: 100 databases; 5 GB storage; 500 million rows read per month; 10 million rows written per month; 3 GB sync | unit: GB | metered on: stored-bytes | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 5 GB across all databases on Free; the plan table gives no per-database cap
- retention: a database is archived after 10 days of inactivity on a free plan, and an archived database must be unarchived before it can be used; a deleted database has no point-in-time restore on Free and the Free column shows 1-day audit logs | days: 10 | source: [2] | note: the archive clock is documented on the CLI and API reference pages, not on the pricing page
- egress: no egress charge and no transfer allowance is published; the metered quantities are rows read and rows written, so a byte of egress is not what is counted | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email signup; GitHub OAuth also offered
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate: 500 million rows read and 10 million rows written per month [1]
  - per-object-cap: 5 GB total across all databases; 100 databases [1]
  - retention-clamped (binding): an inactive database is archived after 10 days on a free plan [2]
  - request-rate: no connection limit is published on the pricing page or the feature pages; recorded as a gap [1]
- binding note: 10 days of inactivity archives the database on the free plan, so a job that runs less often than that finds the database unavailable. The 5 GB total and the 10-million-row monthly write budget are larger than that clock allows a quarterly job to reach.
- interface detail: libSQL over HTTP and WebSockets; the Turso CLI; a platform API
- tooling: the turso CLI; libSQL client libraries; sqld for a local replica
- composes with: a free SQLite replica per tenant suits multi-tenant read-heavy work that a single free Postgres cannot hold, provided something touches each database at least every 10 days, because the free plan archives an inactive one
- reliability: an inactive database on a free plan is archived after 10 days and must be unarchived before use; the archive is not a deletion and the data survives it
- notes: The 500-database and 9-GB figures in circulation are the Developer plan, not Free. The 5 GB is a total, so 100 databases average 50 MB each. The binding constraint is not either number: it is the 10-day archive, which a quarterly job meets first and which nothing on the pricing page states.
- evidence note: the pricing table was read on 2026-10-22 and its own meta description states 100 databases and 5 GB. The 10-day archive clock is from Turso's CLI reference, read the same day; the pricing page does not carry it, so a reader who checks only the pricing page will not find the constraint that binds first.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free column: 100 databases, 5GB storage, 500 Million rows read, 10 Million rows written, 3GB sync, 1 day audit logs; Developer USD 4.99 gives unlimited databases and 9GB
  - [2] 2026-10-22: 'Databases get archived after 10 days of inactivity for users on a free plan'; the unarchive command restores one
  - [3] 2026-10-22: the platform API exposes a group unarchive endpoint, so the archive state is reachable programmatically and not only through the CLI
  - probe:https://api.turso.tech/v1/organizations 2026-10-22: an unauthenticated GET returns 401 with 'token contains an invalid number of segments', proving the platform API exists and is token-authenticated
- sources:
  - [1] https://turso.tech/pricing
  - [2] https://docs.turso.tech/cli/group/unarchive
  - [3] https://docs.turso.tech/api-reference/groups/unarchive

## Upstash Redis (Databases and KV)

- `databases-kv/upstash-redis` | qualifies | evidence measured | binding request-rate | category serverless Redis and KV
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-22
- url https://upstash.com/docs/redis/overall/billing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/upstash.md
- price USD 0.20 per 100K commands; storage USD 0.25/GB-month beyond the first 1 GB | parsed USD 250/TB-mo
- free tier: 250 MB data; 500,000 commands per month; 10 GB bandwidth per month; 10,000 commands per second; one database | unit: mixed | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 100 MB per record on Free; 10 MB per request | source: [1]
- retention: a database on a free account persists while the account is active. An anonymous database created with no account is deleted after 3 days unless claimed | days: 3 | source: [2]
- egress: 10 GB bandwidth per month included on Free; pay as you go includes 200 GB then USD 0.03/GB | metered: yes | free allowance: 10 GB per month | price per TB: USD 0.03/GB beyond 200 GB | source: [1]
- identity: anonymous | detail: POST upstash.com/start-redis with an Idempotency-Key provisions a database with no account, no email and no card; the database is deleted after 3 days unless claimed in a browser. A permanent free database needs an email
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 500,000 commands per month on Free, about 16,600 a day [1]
  - per-object-cap: 100 MB per record; 250 MB total data [1]
  - request-rate (binding): 10 GB bandwidth per month [1]
- limits note: adding a payment method moves every database to paid, and 'an account with a payment method cannot have free databases'
- interface detail: a body-style REST API that takes the command as a JSON array; the Redis protocol on the same endpoint; a developer API
- tooling: redis-cli against the TLS endpoint, or any HTTP client against the REST form; @upstash/redis SDKs
- composes with: the cheapest free cache in front of a free Postgres: 100,000 reads a day off the database, if the write path fits 1,000 a day
- reliability: an unclaimed database carries a warning not to store sensitive data because it is not tied to an account; the documented developer API host api.upstash.com did not resolve on 2026-10-22 while the per-database endpoint worked
- notes: The 10,000-commands-per-day figure in circulation is the pre-2025-03 plan. 500,000 a month is 16,600 a day, which is a different shape: a burst is fine and a steady 1/second is not.
- evidence note: a database was provisioned anonymously, PING/SET/GET/DBSIZE were run against it, and the 3-day expiry was read from the response. The free-plan limits are a first-party page.
- evidence:
  - probe:https://upstash.com/start-redis 2026-10-22: POST with Idempotency-Key 5f4fd5c1-7624-43b4-bfc9-94192920d977 returned 200, 3239 bytes, in 7.0 s, with endpoint optimal-spaniel-201484.upstash.io, a bearer token, a console URL and 'Expires: 2026-10-25 (3 days from creation)'
  - probe:https://optimal-spaniel-201484.upstash.io 2026-10-22: body-style REST calls returned PING -> PONG, SET k1 v1 -> OK, GET k1 -> v1, DBSIZE -> 1; each round trip 0.73 to 0.92 s
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free: 250 MB data, 500K monthly commands, 10 GB monthly bandwidth, 10,000 commands/s, 10 MB request, 100 MB record, 1 database, no credit card
  - probe:https://api.upstash.com/v2/redis/databases 2026-10-22: curl could not resolve api.upstash.com on 2026-10-22, so the documented developer API host is not reachable from this network even though the per-database endpoint is
- sources:
  - [1] https://upstash.com/docs/redis/overall/billing
  - [2] https://upstash.com/start-redis

## Aiven

- `databases-kv/aiven-free` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding retention-clamped | category managed Postgres and friends with a free plan that powers off on inactivity
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://aiven.io/pricing/postgresql | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/aiven.md
- free tier: Free plan with 1 GB RAM and 1 GB total storage per service, on Postgres, MySQL, Valkey, Kafka and OpenSearch; free indefinitely with no time limit, but the service powers off after a period of inactivity | unit: GB | metered on: stored-bytes | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 1 GB total storage per service | source: [1]
- retention: the service powers off after a period of inactivity, on three triggers: no initial usage in the first few hours, or no continuative activity later; a powered-off service is deleted after 180 days. The Free plan is the exception to 'data retention is only limited by storage' | days: 180 | source: [2]
- egress: no egress allowance, quota or per-GB rate is published on the free-plan pages or the PostgreSQL pricing table; recorded as a gap after checking both | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email signup; no card on the Free plan
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - per-object-cap: 1 GB total storage per service; 1 GB RAM [1]
  - retention-clamped (binding): the free service powers off after a period of inactivity; a service powered off for more than 180 days is automatically deleted [2]
  - request-rate: max_connections is set to 20 on a free PostgreSQL service, and there is no connection pooling [3]
- binding note: 1 GB of storage is small, but the inactivity power-off is what defeats the use a reader would pick this for: an unattended job that runs less often than the inactivity window. The 180-day deletion sets the outer limit.
- interface detail: the Postgres wire protocol; an API and the avn CLI
- tooling: psql and any Postgres client; the avn CLI
- composes with: no longer a candidate for a weekly or monthly job: the free service powers off on inactivity and is deleted 180 days after it powers off, so a keep-alive is required and the paid Developer tier is what removes the clock
- reliability: free services power off on inactivity and a service powered off for more than 180 days is automatically deleted; a powered-off service for a version past end of life is deleted within 7…
- notes: 1 GB is the smallest free Postgres storage in this class, and the free plan powers off on inactivity, so it does not answer the question the class was formed to ask. 5 GB is what the plan used to give and several comparison pages still print it. The paid Developer tier at USD 5 a month is the version of this that stays up: 'Developer tier services are not automatically powered off when inactive'.
- evidence note: three first-party Aiven pages were read on 2026-10-22. The pricing page gives 1 GB RAM and 1 GB storage. The free-PostgreSQL page gives the inactivity power-off. The service power-cycle page gives the 180-day deletion. The pricing page's 'with the exception of Free plan' clause is a carve-out and not boilerplate. The free tier is what it carves out.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free column: RAM per VM 1 GB, Total storage 1 GB; Developer USD 5 with 8 GB; Hobbyist from USD 12; 'Data retention is only limited by storage, with the exception of Free plan'
  - [4] 2026-10-22: 'Service powers off after a period of inactivity (you'll be notified by email and in-platform beforehand)'; 'It's free indefinitely with no time limit, but the service is automatically powered off after a period of inactivity'
  - [3] 2026-10-22: two power-off triggers: 'Power off free services with no initial usage within the first few hours after the service is running' and 'Power off free services with no continuative activity on the service'
  - [2] 2026-10-22: 'Services powered off for more than 180 days are automatically deleted'; the 180-day grace does not apply to an end-of-life version, which is deleted within 7 days
  - [5] 2026-10-22: 'Developer tier services are not automatically powered off when inactive'; the paid step is what removes the clock
  - [3] 2026-10-22: 'No connection pooling' and '`max_connections` limit set to `20`' on the free tier
- sources:
  - [1] https://aiven.io/pricing/postgresql
  - [2] https://aiven.io/docs/platform/concepts/service-power-cycle
  - [3] https://aiven.io/docs/products/postgresql/concepts/pg-free-tier
  - [4] https://aiven.io/free-postgresql-database
  - [5] https://aiven.io/docs/platform/concepts/free-plan

## Amazon DynamoDB (dynamodb)

- `databases-kv/dynamodb` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding per-ip-shaping | category key-value and document database
- needs card yes, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/amazon.md
- price USD 0.25/GB-month beyond 25 GB | parsed USD 250/TB-mo
- free tier: 25 GB storage, 25 read capacity units and 25 write capacity units, per region per payer account, always free | unit: GB | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 400 KB per item, which is the DynamoDB engine limit | bytes: 409600 | source: [1]
- retention: data persists while the table exists; no inactivity pause and no expiry clock is published, and the AWS Free Tier page lists DynamoDB under the allowances available on both the 12-month and the always-free plans | source: [2] | note: the 25 GB and 25/25 RCU-WCU figures are the always-free allowance, not a 12-month one, which is what makes the row usable without a countdown
- egress: transfer out is billed; the free tier does not include a transfer allowance for DynamoDB | metered: yes | source: [1]
- identity: card | detail: an AWS account requires a payment instrument
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - per-ip-shaping (binding): 25 read capacity units and 25 write capacity units, equal to 25 strongly-consistent 4 KB reads a second and 25 1 KB writes a second [1]
  - per-object-cap: 25 GB storage per region; 400 KB per item [1]
- limits note: 2.5 million Streams read requests a month are also included
- interface detail: an HTTPS JSON API; the AWS CLI and SDKs; PartiQL
- tooling: boto3, the AWS CLI, any DynamoDB SDK
- composes with: 25 GB that never expires and never pauses, behind an AWS account that needs a card
- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: 25 RCU is the cap, not 25 GB. Twenty-five strongly-consistent reads a second is a prototype's throughput, and 25 GB of storage behind it will never fill.
- evidence note: the pricing page was read; the free tier is stated in its own worked examples.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: 'The AWS Free Tier includes 25 WCUs and 25 RCUs for tables using the DynamoDB Standard table class'; the first 25 GB of storage per region are included; Streams includes 2,500,000 read requests a month
  - [2] 2026-10-22: DynamoDB is listed on the Free Tier page as 'Available on both plans', which places its allowance in the always-free category rather than the 12-month one
- sources:
  - [1] https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/
  - [2] https://aws.amazon.com/free/

## Cloudflare Workers KV

- `databases-kv/cloudflare-kv` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category edge key-value store
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/platform/limits/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/cloudflare.md
- free tier: 100,000 reads per day; 1,000 writes per day; 1 GB per account; 1,000 namespaces | unit: requests | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 25 MiB per value; 512 bytes per key | source: [1] | note: keys per namespace are unlimited, so the value size is the object cap
- retention: no expiry on a stored key unless the write sets one; the free tier does not delete | source: [1]
- egress: reads are counted, not metered by byte; no egress charge on any plan | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: a Cloudflare account
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 1,000 writes per day to different keys [1]
  - request-rate (binding): 1 write per second to the same key [1]
  - per-object-cap: 25 MiB per value; 1 GB per account [1]
- limits note: 100,000 reads per day are unlimited on the paid plan; the minimum cacheTtl is 30 seconds
- interface detail: a REST API and a Worker binding; access through wrangler
- tooling: wrangler kv; the Cloudflare API; a Worker binding in code
- composes with: a read cache in front of a free database: 100,000 reads a day is 100 times the write budget, which is the ratio that makes it a cache and not a store
- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: The asymmetry is the finding: reads are plentiful and writes are not, by two orders of magnitude. Any design that treats KV as the store hits 1,000 writes a day and stops.
- evidence note: the limits page was read; no namespace was created.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free column: 100,000 reads/day, 1,000 writes/day to different keys, 1 write/second to the same key, 1,000 namespaces, 1 GB/account, 1 GB/namespace, 512-byte keys, 25 MiB values, 30-second minimum cacheTtl
- sources:
  - [1] https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/platform/limits/

The vector extension was installed and queried, not merely listed as available, so `pgvector on a free Postgres` is a working chain and not an inference.

- free tier: 50 million query tokens a month, unlimited databases and unlimited tenants per workspace, 1 GB storage included, up to 500 connections, in one region, with no pause on the free tier | unit: tokens | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 1 GB of storage included on Free, then USD 1.50 per additional GB; no per-database cap is published, because the limits are per workspace and split across unlimited databases | bytes: 1000000000 | source: [1]
- retention: no deletion clock is published and the free tier does not pause: 'No, the db never pauses. We don't have any cold start time on the free tier.' The page publishes no inactivity or expiry policy for a free database | source: [1] | note: the free column states 1 day of backup retention; that is a backup window and not a data-retention clock
- egress: no egress allowance and no per-GB transfer line is published; the metered quantity is query tokens and storage | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email signup; no card stated for the Free plan
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 50 million query tokens a month, then USD 0.06 per million additional tokens [1]
  - per-object-cap: 1 GB of storage included, then USD 1.50 per additional GB [1]
  - request-rate (binding): 500 connections on Free; Pro raises it to 10,000 and Scale to 100,000 [1]
- binding note: the token counter is the only hard meter. Storage and connections overage are both purchasable on the free tier without changing plan, and no pause or deletion is published, so the counter is what a reader designs against.
- interface detail: the Postgres wire protocol plus a control-plane API for tenant provisioning
- tooling: psql and any Postgres client; the Nile SDK
- composes with: a multi-tenant Postgres where the tenant count is free and the query volume is the meter, which is the opposite shape from a per-database free tier
- reliability: no pauses and no cold start are claimed on the free tier, and no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: A query token is an abstract unit of CPU and memory. The page defines it but does not convert it, so the allowance cannot be expressed in rows or bytes. That is a discretionary meter in the sense that matters. There is no ceiling a reader can design against, only a price per unit. Two properties make the tier more useful than such a ceiling suggests. The limits are per workspace across unlimited databases, so tenant count is not the constraint. Reaching the limit is an overage and not a refusal. No inactivity or expiry policy is published. The free tier is the only one in this topic where the vendor states that it never pauses.
- evidence note: the pricing page was read for the allowances, the overage rates and the connection counts. The 'never pauses' and the overage-rather-than-refusal answers are the page's own FAQ, read through a search snippet because the collapsed answers do not survive extraction.

  - [2] 2026-10-22: the FAQ answers, captured through the search index because the page renders them collapsed: 'No, the db never pauses. We don't have any cold start time on the free tier.'; 'most limits are per workspace'; 'You can typically pay for additional capacity without having to move to a higher tier. This is true even when you are on the free tier.'

## Supabase (Databases and KV)

- `databases-kv/supabase` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding retention-clamped | category managed Postgres with auth and storage
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://supabase.com/pricing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/supabase.md
- free tier: 500 MB database on Shared CPU with 500 MB RAM; 2 active projects; 5 GB egress and 5 GB cached egress; unlimited API requests | unit: mixed | metered on: stored-bytes | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 500 MB per project database | source: [1]
- retention: a Free project is paused after 1 week of low activity, and is restorable for up to 1 year after the pause. A paid project is never paused | days: 7 | source: [2] | note: the pause trigger is activity, not age: a few user requests a day over the previous week keep it awake
- egress: 5 GB egress and 5 GB cached egress per month included. The Free plan publishes no overage price, so the fifth gigabyte is a wall and not a bill | metered: no | free allowance: 5 GB egress, 5 GB cached egress | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email signup; no card on Free
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - retention-clamped (binding): paused after 1 week of low activity; restorable for up to 1 year [2]
  - per-object-cap: 500 MB per database [1]
  - request-rate: 2 active projects per account; paused projects do not count against the limit [3]
  - request-rate: 5 GB egress per month with no published overage path on Free [1]
  - request-rate: connections are set by the compute size and not published as a single number; the free plan runs Nano compute with up to 0.5 GB of RAM, and the pooler queues above the direct limit rather than raising it [4]
- limits note: the shared pooler is IPv4-only on every plan; a direct connection is IPv6-only without the paid IPv4 add-on, so an IPv4-only host must use the pooler
- interface detail: Postgres wire protocol; a PostgREST data API; a Management API and the Supabase CLI
- tooling: psql and any Postgres client; the supabase CLI; PostgREST over HTTP
- composes with: a free Postgres plus free auth plus free object storage in one project, which is the whole reason to pick it over a bare Postgres
- reliability: two warning emails precede an automatic pause, one about a week ahead and one on the pause; restore is a dashboard action, not an API call on the free plan
- notes: The pause is the finding, and it is a 7-day activity clock rather than a 30-day deletion. A weekly cron that touches the database keeps it alive; a monthly one loses a week of availability every cycle. The restore window is 1 year, so the data is not at risk the way a deletion would put it at risk.
- evidence note: the pricing page and the pausing guide were read; nothing was provisioned. The 90-day restore window stated in the 2024-06-24 changelog has since been widened to 1 year.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: 500 MB database, 2 active projects, 5 GB egress, 5 GB cached egress, 'Free projects are paused after 1 week of inactivity', and the plan table row Pausing: After 1 week of inactivity
  - [2] 2026-10-22: 'Supabase pauses Free Plan projects that show low activity over a 7-day period'; restore is available 'for up to 1 year after it was paused'; a few user requests a day over a week prevent…
  - [3] 2026-10-22: two free projects across all organizations where you are Owner or Administrator; paused projects do not count toward the free project limit
  - [5] 2026-10-22: the 2024-06-24 change set the restore window at 90 days, which the current doc has since widened to 1 year
  - [6] 2026-10-22: the shared Supavisor pooler is multi-tenant and IPv4-only; the dedicated PgBouncer pooler needs a paid plan
  - [4] 2026-10-22: Nano compute is the free plan at USD 0 with up to 0.5 GB of RAM and a recommended 500 MB database; 'Database max connections are recommended values and can be customized via max_connections', so the compute size sets the count
